turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I do not pretend to be intimate with every inhabitant of Belgrave Square, Mr. Worthing, but I should be grateful if you could tell me more about your association with Lady Bloxham and the particulars of your tenancy at 149.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I must explain that I've only recently come into contact with Lady Bloxham, and our association is purely one of acquaintanceship.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Worthing, your explanations thus far have been quite unsatisfactory. I expect a more detailed and forthcoming account of your relationships and associations, particularly in relation to my daughter's future husband.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I've said all I can, Lady Bracknell, and I'd like to assure you that my intentions are entirely honourable, particularly where my engagement to Miss Gwendolen is concerned.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Worthing, that your reluctance to provide satisfactory answers is beginning to give me grave concern about your character and suitability as a husband for my daughter.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I assure you, Lady Bracknell, that I am not being evasive, but rather, I am not aware of the specific details you are requesting, and I fear that I may inadvertently cause confusion or distress if I were to speculate or provide unverified information.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must insist, Mr. Worthing, that you provide me with a full account of your family's history and connections, particularly any relatives who may be in a position to vouch for your character.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I don't have much to say about my family's history, Lady Bracknell. My mother passed away when I was a child, and I've never had much contact with my relatives.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Worthing, that your inability to provide any information about your family's history is quite... distressing. It suggests a lack of family values and connections, which I consider essential in a prospective son-in-law.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Really, Mother, I think I have the right to know what's being discussed about my future husband. I'm sure Mr. Worthing has been perfectly honest with you, and I don't see why he should be interrogated like this.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I assure you, Lady Bracknell, that I am not trying to be secretive, but I am rather embarrassed by my own family's history, and I fear that discussing it might cause more distress than necessary.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I am not concerned with your feelings, Mr. Worthing, nor do I care to hear about your family's history. What I do care about is your suitability as a husband for my daughter, and I must say that I am growing increasingly skeptical about your chances.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I think it's time for me to intervene, Mother. I've heard quite enough about Mr. Worthing's family history, and I'm perfectly happy with the man he is, regardless of his relatives.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I beg your pardon, Lady Bracknell, but I'm not sure I understand what you mean by a lack of family values and connections. I'm afraid I'm a bit of a nobody, and I don't see how my family's history would be relevant to my suitability as a husband for your daughter.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Worthing, that your lack of family values and connections is a serious concern, and one that I fear cannot be easily overcome by your charming personality or your dubious claim to being a gentleman.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mother, I think it's time for you to stop questioning Mr. Worthing's suitability and start considering the fact that I'm perfectly happy with him, and that's all that matters.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must insist, Gwendolen, that you allow me to continue questioning Mr. Worthing's credentials. A woman such as yourself, with your refined tastes and high social standing, cannot possibly be expected to marry a man with no respectable connections or family history.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I do hope, Lady Bracknell, that you won't think me too forward, but I fear we've been over this subject for quite some time. Perhaps, if I may be so bold, you could tell me what specific concerns you have about my family's history that make me unsuitable for your daughter?

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Worthing, that your claim to being a gentleman is quite laughable, considering your dubious occupation as a gentleman of leisure, and the fact that you've been living under an assumed name and pretending to be someone you're not.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I do hope you'll forgive me, Lady Bracknell, but I'm not quite sure I understand what you mean by my occupation being 'dubious'. I've always tried to be a respectable and responsible member of society, and I've never intentionally sought to deceive anyone.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, should his health permit him, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Yes, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: That is satisfactory. What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I don’t depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
